title: Rauchbier and Smoked Beer Guide | Craft Beer School
desc: How malt smoked over a beechwood fire gives rauchbier its bacon like character, and where the technique came from.
teaser: It smells like a bonfire and a lager had an argument. Smoked beer starts with the malt, not the finished brew.
standfirst: Rauchbier gets its smoke from the malt itself, kilned over an open beechwood fire long before it ever reaches the mash tun. That one step is the entire style, and it is far less forgiving than it looks.
sections: Smoke that starts before brewing does

Rauchbier comes from Bamberg in Franconia, Germany, where malt has traditionally been dried over an open beechwood fire rather than the indirect hot air used almost everywhere else today. The smoke penetrates the grain during kilning, depositing phenolic compounds, chiefly guaiacol, that survive mashing, boiling and fermentation and come through clearly in the finished beer.

Because the smoke character is baked into the malt itself, the brewing process afterwards is otherwise ordinary. A rauchbier is not a beer where smoke is added at any later stage, it is simply built from smoked malt the way any other beer is built from its base malt.
Usually a lager underneath the smoke

Most classic rauchbier is based on a Marzen style lager, itself a malt forward, amber, moderately strong style, fermented cold and lagered for weeks before release. The lager base matters, since a clean, cold fermentation leaves nothing competing with the smoke for attention, unlike a fruitier ale yeast might.

Not every smoked beer follows this template. Smoked porters and stouts pair the same smoked malt technique with a dark, roasted ale base, and in Scotland, peat smoked malt, dried over burning peat rather than beechwood, gives a different, earthier smoke character used in some traditional Scotch ales.
What is actually in the glass

Colour typically sits amber to copper, original gravity around 1.050 to 1.057, giving an ABV near 5 percent. Bitterness stays moderate, in the 20 to 30 IBU range, deliberately restrained so it never competes with the smoke. The aroma is the giveaway before a single sip: bacon, campfire and sometimes a faint smoked ham note, backed by the biscuit and toffee malt character typical of a Marzen.
A style that divides opinion on purpose

Rauchbier is one of the few beer styles brewed knowing a large share of drinkers will not like it. In Bamberg, where several breweries have made smoked beer for generations, it is simply the local everyday style, drunk the way a pale lager is drunk anywhere else. Outside that region it tends to be treated as a novelty or a specialist taste, which says more about unfamiliarity than about any fault in the beer.

Smoke intensity in the malt varies noticeably from batch to batch depending on the wood, the fire and how long the kilning ran, since it is a far less precise process than modern indirect kilning. A brewer working with smoked malt has to taste each new batch of grain before brewing and adjust the blend of smoked to unsmoked malt in the grist accordingly, rather than trusting a fixed recipe ratio to deliver a consistent result every time.

Genuine beechwood smoked malt has to be imported, since it is not produced domestically, which makes rauchbier a niche, higher cost style for most Indian breweries to attempt. Some brewers experiment with smoking a portion of their own malt over local wood as an alternative, though the flavour profile will differ from the traditional beechwood character. Serve rauchbier cold, around 6 to 8 degrees Celsius as befits its lager base, and pair it with grilled or barbecued meat, where the smoke in the glass echoes the smoke on the plate.
Tasting it for the first time

Most people either love rauchbier immediately or need a second glass to come around to it, and both reactions are normal. The trick is to stop expecting it to taste like a normal lager with an unusual aftertaste, and instead treat the smoke as the main event, the way you would with a smoked whisky or a barbecued dish. Once the smoke is accepted as the point rather than a flaw to look past, the malt structure and moderate bitterness underneath it become much easier to actually notice and enjoy.
What the style teaches about malt

Rauchbier is one of the clearest demonstrations available that malt is not a neutral, interchangeable ingredient, since the kilning process alone, with nothing else in the recipe changed, can shift a beer's identity entirely. Once a brewer has tasted the difference smoked malt makes at even a modest percentage of the grist, it becomes much harder to think of malt choice as a minor decision behind the more obvious hop and yeast choices, and that shift in thinking carries over into every other style a brewer makes afterwards.
faqs: How does smoke get into rauchbier?
The malt itself is kilned over an open beechwood fire before brewing even begins, so the smoke character comes from the grain rather than being added to the finished beer.
Is rauchbier an ale or a lager?
Most traditional rauchbier is based on a Marzen style lager, fermented cold and lagered for weeks, though smoked malt is also used in some ale styles such as smoked porter.
Bamberg, in the Franconia region of Germany, where several breweries have made smoked beer as their everyday local style for generations.
Why does smoked beer taste different from batch to batch?
Smoked malt is less precisely controlled than standard kilning, so its smoke intensity varies with the wood and fire used, meaning brewers often adjust the grain blend for each new batch.
